Chapter 2: Finding Her Voice—Education, Music, and Early Activism
Picture this—leaving home for the very first time, stepping into a world that feels both thrilling and a little bit overwhelming. That’s exactly what Coretta experienced when she headed off to a boarding school for Black students. The bar was set high, but the resources? Pretty limited. And honestly, the adjustment wasn’t easy. She battled homesickness, moments of doubt, and everything in between. But surrounded by classmates who shared her drive for learning, Coretta started to see herself in a new light. She wasn’t just another student—she realized she actually had a voice, and it mattered.
Through it all, music was her anchor. At school, she truly blossomed, thanks to teachers who believed in her gifts. She sang in choirs, took center stage for solos, and learned how her voice could move people in ways words sometimes couldn’t. For Coretta, music wasn’t just something she did for fun—it was how she connected with others and expressed those deep-down emotions.
After high school, Coretta’s journey took a big leap—she earned a scholarship to Antioch College in Ohio. For a young Black woman from the South, that was a huge deal. The campus felt like a whole new universe. She was meeting people from backgrounds she’d never encountered, and her world opened up in ways she’d only dreamed of. But with that freedom came new hurdles. Discrimination showed up—sometimes hidden, sometimes painfully obvious—but Coretta refused to let it steal her voice.
At Antioch, something shifted. Coretta got involved in student activism, joining campaigns to desegregate local businesses and make the campus more inclusive. These efforts didn’t always win right away. But you know what? That’s where she learned how powerful it is to stand together, and that real change takes time. Setbacks? Part of the process. But giving up? Not an option.
What’s really inspiring is that Coretta’s sense of justice went far beyond her own story. She was deeply moved by the struggles of workers fighting for fair pay, women pushing for equal opportunities, and communities demanding their basic rights. Her activism came straight from the heart—from a place of empathy, and a deep belief that everyone deserves a fair shot.
And here’s where things get even more interesting—music and activism started to blend together. Coretta realized her performances could do more than entertain: they could open eyes, bring people together, and inspire action. She saw firsthand how a single song could break down barriers and give voice to hopes everyone shared. That’s when she began to understand just how unique her role could be—as both an artist and an advocate.
Most folks think leaders just pop up out of nowhere, fully formed. But Coretta’s journey? It proves that leadership grows—one experience at a time. Every challenge she faced, every victory she earned, added a new layer to who she was becoming. So, by the time she graduated, Coretta wasn’t just a girl from Alabama anymore. She was a woman with a purpose, ready to take on whatever the world had in store.
